Simran: I've drafted a list. Chetan, you own the release script. Nidhi, you own testing and the handover note.
Chetan: So if the script breaks, it's mine.
Simran: Yes. And if the handover note is missing, that's Nidhi's.
Nidhi: What should the note look like?
Simran: Three lines: what changed, what's left, who to ask. Same format every time.
Chetan: I can live with that.
Nidhi: Same. Can we put it in the team doc?
Simran: It's already there. Please both reply "confirmed" under it.
Chetan: Confirmed.
Nidhi: Confirmed.
Simran: Good. Next time we start arguing over whose job something was, we open the list instead of the old fight.

qa.q: What three lines does the handover note contain?
qa.a: The note has three lines: what changed, what's left, who to ask.

qa.q: What might Chetan be feeling when asking whether the broken script is Chetan's?
qa.a: Chetan is probably wary about blame, checking what is being asked before agreeing.

qa.q: What else could Simran do so the rules keep working, and why?
qa.a: Simran could review the list with both after a couple of weeks, because roles may need small changes once the work shifts.

qa.q: How might Nidhi see the list?
qa.a: Nidhi probably sees it as fair, since each job has a clear owner and there is one format for the note.

grounding: Illustrates a lead writing a responsibility list, agreeing a handover format and asking both colleagues to confirm, so a rule replaces argument.

subtopic: A conflict between two team members

passage:
Last spring, Ayesha and Rustam were arguing almost daily about the patient-feedback dashboard. Every bug turned into "you should have checked that" and "no, that was your part."
I stopped trying to judge each fight. One evening I opened a blank document and wrote a plain list: Ayesha owns the data pipeline, Rustam owns the charts, I own the release call. Underneath, I added a handover format: three lines, what changed, what might break, who to ask.
The next morning I shared it with both of them and asked each to reply "agreed" or tell me what was wrong. Rustam wanted testing added to his list. Fair. I changed it.
The fights didn't vanish overnight. But when a chart broke two weeks later, Ayesha just checked the handover note, pinged Rustam, and it was fixed by lunch. Nobody asked whose fault it was.
— Zeenat

qa.q: What three lines did the handover format have?
qa.a: What changed, what might break, and who to ask.

qa.q: How might Zeenat have felt when the chart was fixed by lunch with no blame?
qa.a: Zeenat probably felt relieved and quietly satisfied, because the simple list and handover format were doing the work the arguments used to do.

qa.q: Which other approach could Zeenat have used first, and why?
qa.a: Zeenat could have asked why the fights kept starting before writing the list, to check that unclear ownership was really the cause and not something else.

qa.q: How does the responsibility list look to Rustam?
qa.a: Rustam gets a clear area and a chance to change it, so he can ask for testing on his list and stop being blamed for work that was never his.

grounding: It shows a lead writing a simple responsibility list, agreeing a handover format and asking both colleagues to confirm, so the rule replaces arguments about who should have done what.

Supervisor's note — Customer Support Floor 2, Pune office

Observed over three weeks: Ankita, our shift lead, dealing with a running quarrel between Ayesha and Dhruv about escalated tickets. Each said the other was meant to call back angry customers.
Week one, Ankita sat down with a sheet of paper and drew two columns: billing escalations to Ayesha, delivery escalations to Dhruv, anything unclear to herself. She added a handover rule: before leaving, each writes the open ticket number and next step in the shared log.
She printed it and asked both to sign it. Dhruv hesitated, then asked if he could swap Fridays. Ankita agreed and reprinted it.
By week three the corridor arguments had stopped. Ayesha still looked tired, but she told me she no longer dreaded checking the log.
My next step: I've asked Ankita to share the sheet with the other two shifts.

qa.q: How did Ankita split the escalations?
qa.a: Billing escalations went to Ayesha, delivery escalations to Dhruv, and anything unclear to Ankita herself.

qa.q: What does Ayesha saying she no longer dreaded checking the log suggest about how she had felt before?
qa.a: It suggests Ayesha had felt anxious and on edge about the log, expecting a fight over each ticket, and now feels calmer even if still tired.

qa.q: What else could Ankita try if the arguments came back?
qa.a: Ankita could bring Ayesha and Dhruv together with simple ground rules to agree one change each, rather than relying only on the sheet.

qa.q: How does the signed sheet look to Dhruv?
qa.a: Dhruv gets a clear part of the work and a say in it, since he could ask to swap Fridays, so he may feel treated fairly rather than blamed.

grounding: It shows a lead writing a simple responsibility list and handover rule and asking both colleagues to confirm it, as noted by a watching supervisor.
